comparator.sourceNotes: The current official programme page confirms Classics as an integrated study of ancient Greek and Latin language and literature, ancient history, philosophy, archaeology and the later reception of antiquity. The latest complete target-specific official study guide supplies a coherent 180-EC structure: 60 EC in each year. Year 1 combines four 5-EC Greek and Latin acquisition modules with four original-language literature courses and history, philosophy, literary theory and literary history. Year 2 continues original-language prose, drama, epic, linguistics and Renaissance Latin alongside material culture, source transmission, philosophy of science and a restricted thematic choice. Year 3 preserves 30 EC of genuine free-choice space and requires a Greek or Latin workshop, an independent reading list in the other language, late-antique philosophy and religion, and a 10-EC thesis. No formal route or specialization is selected.

exception.reason: Leiden Classics is defined by cumulative ancient Greek and Latin language acquisition, sustained reading of prose and poetry in both original languages, philological and linguistic analysis, and advanced independent reading and research across the two languages. UCR offers valuable study of ancient history, archaeology, philosophy, literature, myth, art and reception, but no Greek or Latin language-acquisition sequence and no curriculum of primary classical texts in the original languages. Those are not peripheral specialist additions: they organize the Leiden programme from the first year through the thesis. A UCR ancient-world pathway would therefore be a defensible Ancient Studies programme, but not a defensible comparator for this language-and-philology-centred Classics degree.
exception.curriculumContext: The latest complete official programme table accounts for exactly 180 EC: 60 EC per year. Year 1 contains 20 EC of Greek and Latin language acquisition and 20 EC of original-language prose, rhetoric, drama and lyric/elegy, integrated with ancient history, philosophy, literary theory and literary history. Year 2 continues Greek and Latin texts, epic, drama, Greek linguistics and Renaissance Latin while adding material culture, source transmission, philosophy of science and a restricted ancient-philosophy choice. Year 3 preserves 30 EC of genuine free choice and requires 15 EC of advanced Greek/Latin reading, late-antique philosophy and religion, and a 10-EC thesis; both classical languages must remain represented.
exception.ucrCourseEvidence: Reviewed all 151 records in the current GitHub main data/reference/ucr_courses_enriched.xlsx (SHA-256 7bf6c2ae9de0837086ec741c27bd94ed7e85dff2d25bde619ecd50cc4d685879), including names, descriptions, outline-derived profiles, disciplines, topics, methods, prerequisites and planned availability. MCCHEAM112 Introduction to World Archaeology, MCCHEAM213 Greek Archaeology, MCCHEAM315 Heritage & Ancient Democracy, GOSHIST213 Western Way of War, GOSPHIL111 Introduction to Western Philosophy, MCCLITR111 Introduction to Literary Studies, MCCLITR112 Great Literary Works and MCCLITR211 World Myth & Literature provide substantial ancient-world, philosophical, literary and material-culture perspectives; MCCHEAM212 Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean and MCCCOMM111 The Art of Rhetorical Communication support reception and rhetoric. The workbook nevertheless contains no ancient Greek course, no Latin course, no cumulative grammar and vocabulary sequence, no sustained original-language reading of Greek and Roman prose and poetry, no classical philology or Greek linguistics sequence, and no advanced Greek/Latin independent reading. Because those missing elements constitute the degree's continuous disciplinary spine, the available ancient-history, archaeology and literature courses support Ancient Studies rather than a defensible Classics match.
